summary: Gives recommendations for using Transport Layer Security with the Network News Transfer Protocol, bringing its use of TLS in line with current best practices. It updates RFC 4642.

eli5.summary: Usenet messages used to travel on open postcards. This tells servers how to put them in a locked envelope the modern way.

questions: which port does nntp over tls use
subtitle: Updates the rules for securing Usenet-style NNTP connections: prefer TLS from the first byte, drop RC4, and follow current TLS best practice.

tldr.problem: RFC 4642 described TLS for NNTP years earlier, and parts of it, such as TLS compression, a mandatory RC4 cipher suite and upgrading via STARTTLS, no longer match today's threat model.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8143 requires NNTP implementations and deployments to follow BCP 195 (RFC 7525), prefers implicit TLS on a dedicated port, and tightens SNI and certificate checking.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 4642 rather than replacing it, and adds client warnings and a defense against STARTTLS command injection.

today: RFC 8143 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4642; the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 8143 itself. It is meant to be read together with RFC 4642 for the full picture of NNTP over TLS.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
NNTP, the Network News Transfer Protocol (RFC 3977), has used TLS and its precursor SSL since at least the year 2000. RFC 4642 formalized this. To address the evolving threat model, RFC 8143 gives stronger recommendations.

Its central rule: NNTP implementations and deployments MUST follow BCP 195, which currently consists of RFC 7525. That covers protocol versions, fallback, TLS negotiation, compression, session resumption, cipher suites, key lengths, forward secrecy, hostname validation and certificate verification. The document then adds NNTP-specific supplementary guidance instead of repeating BCP 195.
sections.eli5: Old advice for locking up news connections had gotten out of date. This RFC says to follow the up-to-date rules for locks and adds a few news-specific tips.

sections.title: What Changes from RFC 4642
sections.content:
The RFC lists five changes to RFC 4642:

  • TLS-level compression SHOULD be disabled, so TLS is no longer used to provide data compression.
  • Implicit TLS is preferred: use a dedicated port and begin TLS negotiation immediately on connection, instead of upgrading dynamically with STARTTLS.
  • RC4 cipher suites MUST NOT be negotiated. The old requirement to implement TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_MD5 is removed; for TLS 1.2 the mandatory suite is TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.
  • All clients, and any server known by multiple names, MUST support Server Name Indication. It was only a SHOULD before.
  • Hostname validation and certificate verification MUST follow RFC 6125 and RFC 5280.
sections.eli5: Five old rules were swapped out: no squeezing data inside the lock, use the locked door from the start, drop a broken lock type, say which house you want to visit, and check IDs properly.

sections.title: Implicit TLS, Ports and STARTTLS
sections.content:
Appendix A.2 replaces text in RFC 4642. TCP port 563 is dedicated to NNTP over TLS. Implementations using it begin TLS negotiation immediately upon connection and then continue with the normal NNTP session. This is called implicit TLS and is the preferred way to use TLS with NNTP.

A host offering separate transit and reading servers SHOULD use port 563 for implicit TLS with the reading server and an unused port of its choice other than 433 for the transit server. Some existing implementations upgrade dynamically with the STARTTLS command on ports 119 or 433, and this RFC formalizes that use but still says to prefer implicit TLS. IPsec with encryption is noted as a common alternative for transit servers without TLS.

To help prevent SSL Stripping, when implicit TLS is not used, news clients SHOULD attempt to negotiate TLS even if the server does not advertise the STARTTLS capability in response to CAPABILITIES.
sections.eli5: The best way is to knock on a door that is always locked, port 563, and start the secret handshake straight away. The older way, starting out in the open and then locking up, is still allowed but is not favored.

sections.title: Compression, Versions and Server Names
sections.content:
NNTP has its own COMPRESS command (RFC 8054). It might be slightly safer than TLS-level compression because it can start after authentication, which lowers the chance of a CRIME-style leak of credentials. The RFC neither encourages nor discourages it.

News servers are encouraged to let administrators set the minimum TLS version and which cipher suites, signature algorithms or groups are used, so they can quickly strengthen security. Clients may offer similar options.

The SNI extension (RFC 6066) MUST be implemented by all news clients and by any news server known by multiple names, because otherwise a server with several hostnames cannot present the correct certificate.
sections.eli5: Servers should let their owners change how strong the lock must be. Clients must say which website name they want, so a server hosting many names can show the right ID.

sections.title: Authentication and Human Factors
sections.content:
Certificate-based authentication with SASL is strongly preferred but not mandated: clients should authenticate servers, servers should authenticate clients, and servers should authenticate peer servers. The AUTHINFO SASL command with the EXTERNAL mechanism MAY authenticate a client after its TLS credentials are exchanged. Citing opportunistic security, the RFC says an encrypted but unauthenticated connection may be better than an unencrypted one.

Clients SHOULD let users, and servers SHOULD let administrators, see whether a connection is encrypted and how it was authenticated. They should also warn about an old TLS version, an unverifiable certificate, a weak cipher suite, a changed certificate, a server that stops advertising STARTTLS after previously advertising it, and a failure response to STARTTLS after it was advertised. The last two tasks cannot occur under implicit TLS.
sections.eli5: Programs should show you whether your connection is locked and warn you when something looks wrong, like a lock that suddenly changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When implicit TLS is not used, servers must guard against the STARTTLS command injection vulnerability. The command MUST NOT be pipelined, but an attacker could pipeline it, so servers MUST discard any NNTP command received between the use of STARTTLS and the end of TLS negotiation.

Other security considerations are those already in RFC 4642, RFC 6125 and BCP 195.
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks extra commands in before the lock is closed, the server must throw them away.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The formal definition of the STARTTLS extension does not change. IANA added a reference to RFC 8143 to the existing STARTTLS label (meaning 'Transport layer security') in the NNTP Capability Labels registry.
sections.eli5: The official list now points to this RFC as well for the STARTTLS entry.
